passage:
Sunday, hostel room 214
Week six. I can make rice without burning it, I got my own SIM fixed, and I found the cheap photocopy shop before anyone else in the wing. Ammi would be shocked. Abbu calls me "our college man" now.
Then tonight the mess served something called biryani and I nearly cried into it. Not because it was bad. Because it wasn't hers. I called home, and Abbu put me on speaker, and I could hear the pressure cooker and my little sister arguing, and I had to go out into the corridor.
Pooja from the next wing found me there and didn't ask anything. She just gave me half her orange.
I thought missing home meant I wasn't ready. Maybe it just means home still counts.
Irfan

passage: The agricultural college hostel stood at the edge of a small town, fields on three sides. By her second month, Jaya had learned to wash her clothes by hand before the water ran out, to catch the six o'clock bus to the library and to bargain at the weekly haat. She felt quietly proud every time. Then one Sunday her brother Gautam arrived on his motorcycle with a steel tiffin from Maa: drumstick sambar, still faintly warm. Jaya opened the lid, and the smell hit her so hard she had to sit down on the step. "Oi, are you crying?" Gautam asked. "No," she said, crying. He sat beside her and ate pickle straight from the jar until she laughed. When he left, she stood at the gate a long time, then went in and tidied her shelf.

passage:
Six weeks into her first term in Edinburgh, Selin, nineteen, had a list on the fridge of things she had done alone: opened a bank account, fixed the radiator valve, found the cheapest bus pass, made lentil soup that tasted almost right. She had phoned her mother in Izmir only twice a week, not every day as she'd feared.
Then on Sunday the flat smelled of someone else's frying onions, and she missed her mother's börek so badly she sat down on the kitchen floor. Her flatmate Mei found her there.
"Homesick?"
"I thought I was past it. It feels so childish."
Mei sat beside her. "I call my grandmother in Taichung every night. I'm not a child. I just love her." Mei held out a dumpling from the pan. "Eat. Then call your mum."
Selin laughed, wiped her face, and called.

qa.q: What had Selin made that tasted almost right?
qa.a: Lentil soup.

qa.q: Why did Selin feel her homesickness was childish?
qa.a: She was proud of managing alone and thought missing her mother's cooking meant she hadn't grown up.

qa.q: What did Mei say that turned the moment around?
qa.a: Mei explained calling a grandmother in Taichung every night out of love, not childishness, showing Selin that missing home is not weakness.

qa.q: How might Selin's mother feel getting that Sunday call?
qa.a: She would likely feel glad and close to Selin, since the call shows their bond is still strong.

grounding: A first-year student abroad is proud of managing alone yet aches for her mother's cooking, and learns that missing home shows the bond remains.

passage:
The engineering college mess served sambar again, the fourth night running, and Farhan, eighteen, pushed his rice around. Two months ago he had arrived in Tiruchirappalli from Lucknow knowing nobody. Now he could wash his clothes, fix his cycle chain and argue with the warden about hot water. He was proud of all of it.
His phone buzzed: a video call from his sister Afreen. Behind her was their kitchen, Ammi frying kebabs, Abbu's radio. The sound of home went straight through him. His throat closed.
"Are you crying in the mess?" Afreen asked.
"No. Maybe. I'm fine, it's stupid."
Ammi leaned into the screen. "Stupid? My son misses my kebabs. That's the best news I've had all week."
Farhan laughed, wiped his eyes on his sleeve, and made them carry the phone round the whole kitchen.

qa.q: What was Ammi frying during the video call?
qa.a: She was frying kebabs.

qa.q: Why did Farhan's throat close when he saw the kitchen?
qa.a: The familiar sounds of home stirred a sudden ache of missing his family, even though he had been proud of managing alone.

qa.q: How did Ammi's response help Farhan?
qa.a: By calling his homesickness the best news, she showed him that missing home is a sign of love, not weakness.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel seeing her brother tear up in the mess?
qa.a: She may feel tender and protective, and glad that he still misses them.

grounding: A hostel student proud of managing alone suddenly aches for home during a video call, and his mother treats the missing as a sign of the bond.

passage: Looking back now, the thing I remember about my first term in Delhi isn't the classes. It's the second Sunday. I'd done well all week: opened a bank account, found the laundry, argued with the auto driver and won. I felt tall. Then in the mess they served rajma, and it smelt nothing like Minakshi-maasi's. I went back to my room and cried into my pillow for an hour. I was eighteen and embarrassed; I thought real adults don't cry over beans. I didn't tell anyone. That night I called home, just to hear the TV in the background, my father coughing, my maasi scolding the dog. I didn't even say I was sad. I just listened. Only later did I understand that the ache wasn't weakness. It meant the people back home were still part of me. I'm Rajni, and I still call on Sundays.

qa.a: The mess served rajma.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel after crying over the rajma?
qa.a: Rajni felt embarrassed, thinking real adults don't cry over beans, and homesick for maasi's cooking and home voices.

qa.q: What did Rajni do that night that helped, and why?
qa.a: Rajni called home just to listen to familiar sounds, which eased the ache without needing to explain it.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, Room 214, Thursday.
Vinita (first year, from Shillong) has settled well on the surface. She sorted her own SIM card, found the cheapest laundry, and helped two girls on her floor with their forms. She tells everyone she's "fine, totally independent." Tonight after dinner I found her sitting on the stairwell, eyes red, holding a steel tiffin her mother had packed weeks ago. She said the mess dal tasted wrong and she could not stop thinking about her grandmother's voice. She apologised for "being a baby." I told her missing home meant she had a good home to miss. We rang her mother together from my office phone. Vinita laughed at something within a minute. I've asked the mess to add a Sunday choice from the students' home states and will check on her again at breakfast.
- Francis, Warden

passage:
Diary, Saturday night

Two months in the hostel in Pune. I, Irfan, am doing well. I cook my own instant noodles, I do my own laundry, I even fixed the fan in our room. My roommate Abhinav calls me "the engineer".
Today I felt proud all day. Then at dinner, the mess served dal that tasted nothing like Ammi's. Suddenly I missed everything: her voice calling me for chai, my sister's teasing, the smell of our old house.
I cried a bit in the bathroom. Felt stupid.
Abhinav noticed my eyes. He said, "I miss my mum's food too, yaar. Every day."
It helped. Maybe missing home isn't weakness. Maybe it just means I still belong there.

Jatin had been at the agricultural college in Dharwad for three months, living in a small hostel near the fields. He was proud: he'd learned to use the tractor, organised the hostel mess rota and topped his first soil exam.
But on the night of the village fair back home, he could hear, faintly, drums from a festival in the next town. He sat on the hostel steps and felt his chest ache. He missed his Amma's jowar rotis, his grandfather's stories, the noise of the fair.
The warden, Manjula Ma'am, found him there. "Homesick?"
Jatin nodded, embarrassed.
"Good," she said. "It means they matter. Now come, there's rotis in the kitchen. Not your Amma's. But warm."

But the chhole was too sweet, not like Ma's in Kolkata, and suddenly the whole noisy mess felt enormous. She pushed her plate away. Her phone buzzed: a voice note from her little brother Pranav, singing a terrible birthday song for their dog. Sharmila laughed out loud and then cried a little into her dupatta, right there at the long table. A senior at the next table slid a packet of nimki across without a word. Sharmila played Pranav's voice note four more times before bed.

I'm so proud of myself I could burst. But can I tell you something embarrassing? Missing everything and fine at the same time,
Yamini
